**Decisions I made without you** (all recorded in `work/protocol.json`):
- **Outcome as a search block:** small vessel disease is treated as the exposure and dementia/cognition as the outcome. I included the outcome as a search block because small vessel disease papers cover many other outcomes (stroke, gait, mood, mortality). I kept that block very broad, and removing it would not recover any of the known studies.
- **Left to screening:** cohort design, community setting, incidence and MRI are not searched.
- **Cutting noise:** the first draft retrieved 19,500 records. Most of the reduction came from requiring MRI wording alongside three broad stroke/haemorrhage headings, which were bringing in acute-stroke papers. No known study was lost at any step.
- **Review rounds:** two fresh-context review rounds checked the strategy against the PRESS checklist. This was an automated internal check, not PRESS peer review. Every finding was fixed or answered with a stated reason. The main one I rejected was adding the White Matter heading: tested, it added 507–849 records of brain-connectivity (DTI) and psychiatric studies and nothing relevant.

**Risks for the reviewer:**
- **Screening load:** most of it comes from the broad cognition terms (Neuropsychological Tests, memory, information processing). If 12,495 records is too many, test removing those against the known studies before adding any study-design block.
- **Under-represented markers:** the earlier reviews focused on white matter hyperintensities and microbleeds, so studies about only lacunes or perivascular spaces are thinly represented in the known sets.
- **CT-based studies:** studies of white matter lesions seen on CT are retrieved, but the eligibility criteria specify MRI markers. Whether to include them is a screening decision.
- **PubMed only:** a systematic review also needs Embase and other sources.

Files are in `./work`:
- audit.md
- protocol.json
- strategy.json
